etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English varien, from Old French varier, from Latin variō (“to change, alter, make different”), from varius (“different, various”); see various.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To change with time or a similar parameter.

quote.citation: 1695, C[harles] A[lphonse] du Fresnoy, translated by John Dryden, De Arte Graphica. The Art of Painting, […], London:  […]  J[ohn] Heptinstall for W. Rogers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: We are to vary the customs according to the time and country where the scene of action lies.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To institute a change in, from a current state; to modify.

quote.text: Gods, that never change their state, / Vary oft their love and hate.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) Not to remain constant: to change with time or a similar parameter.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene iii, page 1:
quote.text: While fear and anger, with alternate grace, / Pant in her breast, and vary in her face.

definitions.definition: (of the members of a group, intransitive) To display differences.

quote.citation: 1960 February, “The modernisation of Peterborough”, in Trains Illustrated, page 108:
quote.text: In the new layout, it is proposed to provide three island platforms with six platform faces varying from 1,075 to 1,290 ft. in length and including bays.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be or act different from the usual.
(transitive) To make of different kinds; to make different from one another; to diversify; to variegate.

quote.citation: 1650, Thomas Browne, Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  A[braham] Miller, for Edw[ard] Dod and Nath[aniel] Ekins, […], →OCLC:

1667, John Milton, “Book V”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: God hath here / Varied his bounty so with new delights.

definitions.definition: (transitive, music) To embellish; to change fancifully; to present under new aspects, as of form, key, measure, etc. See variation.
(intransitive, obsolete) To disagree; to be at variance or in dissension.

quote.citation: 1623, John Webster, The Devil's Law Case:
quote.text: the rich jewel which we vary for

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: With euery gall, and varry of their Masters,
